questions.qtext: Suppose a directed graph has no negative cycles. You run the Bellman-Ford algorithm from a source $S$. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The shortest-path distances from $S$ are always the same, no matter the order of edge relaxations.
The exact shortest-path tree chosen is always the same, no matter the order of edge relaxations.
If a vertex can be reached by two different shortest paths of equal length, the chosen path may depend on relaxation order.
If each vertex has exactly one shortest path from $S$, then the shortest-path tree will not depend on the relaxation order.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Scenario: Directed graph with no negative cycles.

Analysis:

  • A. The shortest-path distances... are always the same...

    • Correct. Shortest path distances are a mathematical property of the graph. As long as there are no negative cycles, the distance is well-defined and unique. Bellman-Ford is guaranteed to find this unique distance regardless of relaxation order.

  • B. The exact shortest-path tree chosen is always the same...

    • Incorrect. If there are multiple paths with the same minimum length, the algorithm might pick one or the other depending on the order in which edges are relaxed.

  • C. If a vertex can be reached by two different shortest paths... chosen path may depend on relaxation order.

    • Correct. (This is the complement of statement B).

  • D. If each vertex has exactly one shortest path... shortest-path tree will not depend on relaxation order.

    • Correct. If the path is unique, the algorithm has no choice but to converge on that single specific tree.

Correct Option: A, C, and D are correct.

questions.qtext:
Recall the update operation on distances in the Bellman-Ford algorithm:
$$
\operatorname{update}(u \rightarrow v): \quad \operatorname{dist}[v]=\min (\operatorname{dist}[v], \operatorname{dist}[u]+\ell(u, v))
$$
Consider the following graph:
$$
S \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow B
$$
If all edge weights are positive, which is the shortest sequence of update operations that ensures all distances from $S$ are correctly computed, irrespective of the edge weights?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

The update operation is: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + l(u, v))

This operation can only find the final shortest-path distance for v if the distance to the previous node, dist[u], is already correct.

S → A → B
We start with dist[S] = 0. All other distances are initialized to infinity: dist[A] = ∞, dist[B] = ∞. The only path to A is S → A. To calculate dist[A], we must use the update(S → A) operation. This requires dist[S] to be correct (which it is, at 0). The only path to B is S → A → B. To calculate dist[B] using the update(A → B) operation, we must have the correct value for dist[A].

Answer: B

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

🔹 The Question Setup

We have a directed graph:

S → A → B

All edges have positive weights.
Let’s denote them as:

  • weight(S → A) = w₁

  • weight(A → B) = w₂

We want to know:

What is the shortest sequence of edge relaxations that ensures all shortest distances from S are correctly computed, no matter what the weights are?

💡 Step 1: Recall the Bellman–Ford update rule

For each edge ( u \to v ):
[
\text{dist}[v] = \min(\text{dist}[v], \text{dist}[u] + w(u, v))
]

That means we use the current knowledge of dist[u] to try to improve dist[v].

But — this only works if dist[u] is already correct (or at least smaller than before).

So, information (shortest distance) flows from source → outward, one edge at a time.

🌱 Step 2: Start from what we know

Initially:

dist[S] = 0
dist[A] = ∞
dist[B] = ∞

The source (S) is the only vertex whose distance is known correctly at the start.

⚙️ Step 3: Propagation of shortest path info

To get the correct distance for A:

  • We must relax the edge S → A.

Then:

dist[A] = min(∞, dist[S] + w₁)
dist[A] = 0 + w₁ = w₁

✅ Now we know the true shortest distance to A.

To get the correct distance for B,
we need the value of dist[A] (because A lies between S and B).

So next, we relax A → B:

dist[B] = min(∞, dist[A] + w₂)
dist[B] = w₁ + w₂

✅ Now we know the true shortest distance to B.

🧩 Step 4: Understanding the dependency chain

Let’s think in terms of information flow:

S → A → B

  • To compute A’s shortest distance, we depend on S.

  • To compute B’s shortest distance, we depend on A (which depends on S).

So the relaxation order must “respect” this dependency.

That means:
[
S \to A \text{ must come before } A \to B
]

Otherwise, B would get updated based on an incorrect (infinite) value of A.

⚡ Step 5: Check each option intuitivelyOption A: A → B, S → A

❌ Wrong.

If we relax A → B first:

  • dist[A] is still ∞

  • So dist[B] doesn’t get updated.

Then after S → A, A becomes correct — but B remains outdated.

We’d need another relaxation on A → B → Not the shortest sequence.

Option B: S → A, A → B

✅ Correct.

1️⃣ Relax S → A:
Now A has correct distance.
2️⃣ Relax A → B:
Now B gets its correct distance.

Done! All distances are now correct — with the shortest possible 2 relaxations.

Option C: S → A only

❌ Wrong.

B never gets updated.
dist[B] stays ∞.

Option D: A → B, S → A, S → B

❌ Unnecessary relaxations — we already get everything done with Option B.

✅ Final Answer:

Option B — (S → A, A → B)
is the shortest sequence that guarantees all distances from S are computed correctly, for any positive weights.

🌟 Intuitive Summary

Bellman–Ford’s correctness depends on the order of dependency —
you can think of it as wavefront propagation from the source outward.

For the path:

S → A → B

The correct information flow order is the same as a topological order of edges:
[
(S → A) \text{ before } (A → B)
]

That ensures each node’s shortest path is finalized before its children are relaxed.

💎 GATE-level Insight

This is why Bellman–Ford (and DAG shortest path) can often be optimized:

  • In general, you relax all edges |V|−1 times.

  • But if you relax edges in topological order (like in this example),
    you need only one pass! 🚀

🔚 Key takeaway
ConceptMeaning
Relaxation order mattersYou must relax an edge only after the source node’s distance is correct
In chain graph S→A→BRelax S→A first, then A→B
Relation to topological orderWorks perfectly for acyclic graphs (DAGs)

Would you like me to show how this idea generalizes to a larger DAG (e.g., S→A→B→C→D) — where only one linear pass (topological order) gives all shortest paths instantly?
That’s one of the most elegant insights about Bellman–Ford vs DAG shortest path.

The figure above shows an undirected graph. Dijkstra's algorithm is being run from source s.

Edges already in the current shortest-path tree are drawn solid; the remaining edges are dashed.

Which dashed edge will be added next to the shortest-path tree by Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

From the figure, the solid edges already in the shortest-path tree are:

  • $s \rightarrow v 5$ with weight 1

  • $v 5 \rightarrow v 6$ with weight 1

  • $v 5 \rightarrow v 2$ with weight 2

  • $v 2 \rightarrow v 3$ with weight 1


So far, the shortest-path distances are:

  • $d(s)=0$

  • $d(v 5)=1$

  • $d(v 6)=d(v 5)+1=2$

  • $d(v 2)=d(v 5)+2=3$

  • $d(v 3)=d(v 2)+1=4$


Now check the dashed frontier edges:

  • ( $\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{v} 1$ ) with weight $7 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=0+7=7$

  • ( $\mathrm{v} 1, \mathrm{v} 2$ ) with weight $3 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=3+3=6$

  • (v6, v7) with weight $3 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=2+3=5$

  • ( $\mathrm{v} 2, \mathrm{v} 3$ ) with weight $2 \rightarrow$ already in the tree, ignore


The smallest tentative distance is from ( $\mathbf{v 6}, \mathbf{v 7}$ ) with total distance $5$.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Based on the Dijkstra's algorithm simulation on the provided graph:

  1. Identify the current state:

    The problem states that solid edges are already in the shortest-path tree (SPT). Let's determine the visited vertices and their shortest path distances from the source s based on these solid edges:

    • s: Distance = 0

    • v5: Connected via (s, v5) with weight 1. Distance $d[v5] = 0 + 1 = \mathbf{1}$.

    • v6: Connected via (v5, v6) with weight 1. Distance $d[v6] = d[v5] + 1 = 1 + 1 = \mathbf{2}$.

    • v2: Connected via (v5, v2) with weight 2. Distance $d[v2] = d[v5] + 2 = 1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}$.

    • v3: Connected via (v2, v3) with weight 1. Distance $d[v3] = d[v2] + 1 = 3 + 1 = \mathbf{4}$. (Note: The path via v6 would be $2+4=6$, so the path via v2 is indeed shorter).

    So, the set of vertices already in the SPT is {s, v5, v6, v2, v3}.

  2. Evaluate candidate edges for the next step:

    Dijkstra's algorithm always picks the "dashed" edge that connects a vertex in the SPT to a vertex outside the SPT such that the total distance from the source is minimized. The unvisited vertices are v1, v4, and v7.

    Let's calculate the potential distance for each unvisited neighbor:

    • To reach v1:

      • Via edge (s, v1) (weight 7): Distance = $d[s] + 7 = 0 + 7 = 7$.

      • Via edge (v2, v1) (weight 3): Distance = $d[v2] + 3 = 3 + 3 = 6$.

      • Minimum distance to v1 is 6.

    • To reach v4:

      • Via edge (v3, v4) (weight 2): Distance = $d[v3] + 2 = 4 + 2 = \mathbf{6}$.

    • To reach v7:

      • Via edge (v6, v7) (weight 3): Distance = $d[v6] + 3 = 2 + 3 = \mathbf{5}$.

      • (Note: v4 is not visited yet, so we cannot use the edge (v4, v7)).

  3. Select the minimum:

    Comparing the best distances to all reachable unvisited nodes:

    • $v1: 6$

    • $v4: 6$

    • $v7: 5$

    The minimum distance is 5. The algorithm will select vertex v7 next. The edge that provides this minimum distance is (v6, v7).

  4. Check the options:

    • A. Edge (s, v1) with weight 7: Incorrect.

    • B. Edge (v1, v2) with weight 3: Incorrect (result distance 6).

    • C. Edge (v6, v7) with weight 3: Correct (result distance 5).

    • D. Edge (v2, v3) with weight 2: Incorrect. This edge is already solid (part of the tree), and its weight in the diagram is 1, not 2.

Correct Answer: C. Edge (v6, v7) with weight 3

questions.qtext:
There are $n$ magic portals in a game.

  • If you enter portal $i$, it can send you to portal $j$.
  • Your power gets multiplied by $T[i][j]$.

Thus, if you follow a sequence of portals
$$
i_{1} \rightarrow i_{2} \rightarrow i_{3} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow i_{k} \rightarrow i_{1},
$$
then the final power is
$$
P=T\left[i_{1}\right]\left[i_{2}\right] \cdot T\left[i_{2}\right]\left[i_{3}\right] \cdots \cdots T\left[i_{k}\right]\left[i_{1}\right] .
$$
We want to check if there exists a cycle of portals such that the final power $P>1$.

We want to somehow use the Bellman-Ford algorithm feature of detecting negative cycles here. We will say: if there is a negative cycle, then final power $P>1$.

For this, we must define the edge weight $w(i, j)$ for each directed edge $(i \rightarrow j)$. Which of the following definitions is correct?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

Take option D:
$$
w(i, j)=-\log (T[i][j]) .
$$

In Bellman-Ford, when we go around a cycle, we add weights.

So for a cycle, the total weight becomes:
$$
-\log (T[i][j] \cdot T[j][k] \cdot T[k][i]) .
$$

  • If this value is negative, then

$$
\log (T[i][j] \cdot T[j][k] \cdot T[k][i])>0 .
$$

  • And if $\log$ is positive, it means the product is greater than 1.


In other words:

  • If the product is just a fraction (< 1 ), log is negative

  • If the product is $>1$, $\log$ is positive.


So, a negative cycle in Bellman-Ford means the product > 1, i.e. your power increases after the cycle.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Answer is D
Understanding the Problem

In this game, every time we move through a portal, our power is multiplied by the value on that edge. If we complete a cycle, the final power is the product of all the edge values in that cycle:

$$P = T[i_1][i_2] \cdot T[i_2][i_3] \cdots T[i_k][i_1]$$

We want to know if there is a cycle where the power increases, which means

$$P > 1.$$


Why We Cannot Use the Edge Values Directly

The question asks us to use the Bellman-Ford algorithm. The problem is that Bellman-Ford works by adding edge weights, not multiplying them.

If we use the original values $T[i][j]$, the algorithm will only calculate their sum, but our condition depends on their product. So, we need a way to convert multiplication into addition.


Using Logarithms

Logarithms help because they change multiplication into addition:

$$\log(a \cdot b) = \log(a) + \log(b).$$

If we replace every edge weight with its logarithm, then the sum of the edge weights around a cycle becomes

$$\log(P).$$

Our original condition is

$$P > 1.$$

Taking the logarithm of both sides gives

$$\log(P) > \log(1).$$

Since $\log(1) = 0$,

$$\log(P) > 0.$$

So after applying logarithms, we are looking for a cycle whose total weight is greater than zero, i.e., a positive cycle.


Why This Still Does Not Work

Bellman-Ford is designed to find the shortest paths. It can detect negative cycles, but it does not detect positive cycles.

A positive cycle only increases the total path cost, so the algorithm simply ignores it. On the other hand, a negative cycle keeps reducing the path cost, so Bellman-Ford can recognize that something is wrong and reports its existence.

Since our cycle has a positive sum, we need to convert it into a negative one.

Converting It into a Negative Cycle

Starting from

$$\log(P) > 0,$$

multiply both sides by $-1$. Remember that multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality:

$$-\log(P) < 0.$$

Now define the weight of each edge as

$$w(i, j) = -\log(T[i][j]).$$

With this change, any cycle that increases the player's power becomes a negative-weight cycle. Bellman-Ford can detect this negative cycle, allowing us to determine whether such a power-increasing cycle exists.

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

What is actually happening in the game?

  • You go through portals

  • Each portal multiplies your power

  • After a cycle, your power becomes:

\[P = T[i_1][i_2] × T[i_2][i_3] × ... × T[i_k][i_1]\]
If there is a negative cycle then $P>1$,
\[ P>1\]
\[ T[i_1][i_2] × T[i_2][i_3] × ... × T[i_k][i_1]>1\]
We want to detect this negative cycle.
However in this example every time we cycle the power increases(multiplied)
Bellman Ford can only detect a negative cycle if there is a decrease(we something that is negative, so that in Vth iteration there is another relaxation)
To achieve this negative behavior we can apply -log to convert the product to a sum that yields a negative results.
\[w(i,j) = -log(T[i][j])\]
\[ -log(T1) + -log(T2) + ... > -log(1) \]
Example:
Suppose a cycle leads to $2 × 0.5 × 2 = 2 > 1$ (negative cycle)
For Bellman Ford to detect this, we apply $-log$
$-log(2) -log(0.5) -log(2)$
$≈ -0.69 +0.69 -0.69 = -0.69$ (negative result that will cause some decrease)

Why other options are wrong:
+log will create +ve weight cycles which Bellman-Ford can't detect
Using T or −T does not convert multiplication into addition, so Bellman–Ford cannot reason about the cycle.
